title: Outs and the rule of 2 and 4
summary: How many cards improve your hand and how to estimate your chances fast.

outs.text:
**Outs** are the unseen cards that will most likely make your hand the best one. The common cases:
- **Flush draw** (four cards of a suit): 13 − 4 = **9 outs**.
- **Open-ended straight draw** (OESD, four in a row): **8 outs**, four on each end.
- **Gutshot** (missing a card in the middle): **4 outs**.
- **Two overcards** to the board: up to **6 outs**, but dirty ones.
- **Combo draw** (flush plus straight): up to **15 outs**.

labels: Combo draw: 15 outs (9 hearts + 3 queens and 3 sevens that are not hearts)

rule.text:
The **rule of 2 and 4** turns outs into percentages:
- On the **flop**, when you will see both remaining cards (say, someone is all-in): outs × **4**.
- With one card to come (flop to turn, or turn to river): outs × **2**.

A flush draw on the flop: 9 × 4 ≈ 36% (exactly 35%). On the turn: 9 × 2 ≈ 18% (exactly 19.6%).

With many outs the rule of 4 overshoots: subtract (outs − 8). For 15 outs: 60 − 7 = 53% (exactly 54%).

q-turn.q: You have an open-ended straight draw on the turn. Your chance to hit on the river is about?
q-turn.explain: 8 outs × 2 = 16% (exactly 8/46 ≈ 17.4%). Only one card is left, so ×2, not ×4.

dirty.text: Not all outs are clean. A card may give you a hand but make your opponent's even stronger: your straight loses to a flush when three cards of a suit are on the board. Count such outs partly or not at all. Overcards are especially dirty: pairing your ace only helps when your opponent doesn't hold a better pair.

t1.q: How many outs does a flush draw have?
t1.explain: A suit has 13 cards, four are already seen: 9 are left.

t2.q: A flush draw on the flop, and your opponent moves all-in. Your chance to make the flush by the river is about?
t2.explain: Turn and river are both to come: 9 × 4 ≈ 36%, exactly 35%.

t3.q: How many outs does a gutshot have?
t3.explain: You need one specific rank, and there are four of it in the deck.
